title: Top Local Payment Methods in Malaysia: How Malaysians Pay
summary: From FPX and DuitNow to Touch ’n Go and cards, see how Malaysians pay online and in store, and how to accept the top methods with one integration. The post Top Local Payment Methods in Malaysia: How Malaysians Pay appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Malaysians pay digitally more often every year. In 2025, the average Malaysian made 538 e-payments, and no single method dominates checkout: shoppers move between online banking, e-wallets, QR codes, cards, and buy now, pay later (BNPL) depending on what they buy and where. For merchants, the lesson is simple: a card-only checkout misses most Malaysian shoppers.


This guide covers the six payment method categories that matter most in Malaysia, who uses each one, and when to offer it, along with a recommended payment mix by business type. Each section links to our in-depth guide for that category.


Key takeaways:


- Bank payments through FPX and DuitNow are the backbone of online checkout, accounting for 44% of e-commerce value in 2025.


- E-wallets are part of everyday spending, with 26% of e-commerce value and 32% of point-of-sale value in 2025.


- DuitNow QR transactions doubled to 3 billion in 2025, and one national QR code accepts payments from any participating bank or e-wallet app.


- Cards remain essential for bigger tickets, subscriptions, and international customers, and installment plans help lift conversion on large purchases.


- Offer both FPX and at least one major e-wallet on every consumer checkout, since each covers shoppers the other misses.


## **How Malaysians pay today**


Malaysians have moved quickly to digital payments. Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) recorded 18.4 billion e-payment transactions in 2025, up 25% from 2024, which works out to 538 e-payments per person over the year, according to the


[BNM Annual Report 2025](https://www.bnm.gov.my/publications/ar2025/ch1e) . DuitNow QR transactions doubled to 3 billion over the same period.


Unlike card-led markets, no single method dominates checkout in Malaysia. Bank transfers through FPX and DuitNow are the backbone of online payments, e-wallets have become part of everyday spending, and cards remain important for bigger tickets and international shoppers. Nearly three in five Malaysians had paid digitally in the past three months, according to a December 2025 Ipsos study \[link needed\].


Much of this runs on PayNet, the national payments network behind FPX, DuitNow, and MyDebit. PayNet processed


[8.44 billion digital transactions in 2025](https://paynet.my/about-us/media-centre/press-release/8-44-billion-transactions-processed-in-2025-as-digital-payments-become-malaysians-preferred-way-to-pay.html) .

### **1. Online banking: FPX and DuitNow Pay**


Paying straight from a bank account is the most common way Malaysians check out online. Account-to-account payments through FPX and DuitNow accounted for 44% of e-commerce value in 2025, the largest share of any method, according to the


[Global Payments Report 2026](https://fintechnews.sg/128337/e-commerce/southeast-asia-payment-methods-2026-global-payments-report/) . Mobile banking is now the preferred online banking channel, with a 64% share,


[according to BNM](https://www.malaymail.com/news/money/2026/03/31/contactless-and-duitnow-qr-transactions-rise-25pc-in-2025-malaysians-make-538-payments-each-on-average/214496) .


There are two rails to know:


- FPX (Financial Process Exchange):


PayNet's long-established online banking gateway. The customer picks their bank, logs in, and approves. It has separate retail and corporate channels, so it also works for business-to-business payments.


- DuitNow Pay (DuitNow Online Banking/Wallets):


PayNet's newer open-banking checkout that lets customers authorize payment from their preferred bank account, including digital banks such as Boost Bank.


How it works:


the customer selects their bank at checkout, is redirected to their bank's app or site, and approves the payment. Confirmation is instant, and there is no card or wallet top-up involved.


When to offer it:


always, if you sell online in Malaysia. FPX is the default for higher-value consumer purchases, insurance, education fees, and B2B orders. With Xendit,


[FPX](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/online-banking) covers 40 channels across 23 banks, with limits up to RM30,000 on retail accounts and RM1 million on corporate accounts.


[DuitNow Pay](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/duitnow-pay) supports payments from RM1 to RM30,000 with full and partial refunds.


*Read also:*[FPX Payments in Malaysia: A Complete Guide for Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-my/blog/fpx-payments-in-malaysia-a-complete-guide-for-businesses/)


### **2. E-wallets: part of everyday life**


Digital wallets accounted for 26% of e-commerce value and 32% of point-of-sale value in 2025, according to the


[Global Payments Report 2026](https://fintechnews.sg/128337/e-commerce/southeast-asia-payment-methods-2026-global-payments-report/) . Malaysians use them for tolls, parking, transit, food, and online shopping. The average e-money transaction grew from RM33 in 2024 to RM43 in 2025, a sign that people now trust wallets for bigger purchases too,


The wallets that matter most:


- Touch 'n Go eWallet:


grew from highway tolls into an everyday super app for transit, retail, bills, and transfers. It has the broadest reach for local consumer spending.


- GrabPay:


tied to the Grab ecosystem of rides, food delivery, and rewards.


- ShopeePay:


the go-to wallet for Shopee shoppers and promo-driven online purchases.


- Boost and MAE by Maybank:


popular local options, the latter linked directly to a Maybank account.


- WeChat Pay and Alipay:


the preferred payment methods of many visitors from China, important for tourism, retail, and F&B.


How it works:


the customer picks a wallet at checkout, is redirected to the app, and confirms with a PIN or biometrics. Payment is confirmed instantly.


When to offer it:


for consumer-facing businesses, especially F&B, retail, transport, digital goods, and anything bought on mobile. With Xendit, you can accept


[Touch 'n Go](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/touch-n-go) ,


[GrabPay](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payment-channel-page-pull-4) ,


[ShopeePay](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/my-shopeepay) ,


[WeChat Pay](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/my-wechatpay) , and Alipay. Touch 'n Go, GrabPay, and ShopeePay can also be saved for recurring and one-click payments. Limits vary by wallet, from RM1,500 on GrabPay up to RM30,000 on ShopeePay.


*Read also:*[E-Wallets in Malaysia: A Complete Guide for Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-my/blog/e-wallets-in-malaysia-a-complete-guide-for-businesses-accepting-digital-payments/)


### **3. DuitNow QR: one national QR code**


DuitNow QR is Malaysia's national QR standard, run by PayNet. One code accepts payment from any participating bank app or e-wallet, so merchants do not need a separate QR for each provider.


It is the fastest-growing way to pay in person. DuitNow QR transactions doubled from 1.5 billion in 2024 to 3 billion in 2025, according to the


[BNM Annual Report 2025](https://www.bnm.gov.my/publications/ar2025/ch1e) , and there were


[more than 3 million registered DuitNow QR touchpoints](https://paynet.my/about-us/media-centre/press-release/8-44-billion-transactions-processed-in-2025-as-digital-payments-become-malaysians-preferred-way-to-pay.html) across Malaysia by the end of 2025.


DuitNow QR also works across borders. It links with Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, China, and Cambodia, with India expected in 2026, and


[cross-border QR transactions grew 2.5 times to 29.7 million in 2025](https://paynet.my/about-us/media-centre/press-release/8-44-billion-transactions-processed-in-2025-as-digital-payments-become-malaysians-preferred-way-to-pay.html) .


How it works:


the customer scans the merchant's QR code with their banking or wallet app and confirms the amount. Payment is instant.


When to offer it:


for physical stores, hawkers and F&B, events, and any business that serves tourists from linked countries. It is the simplest way to accept payments from every bank and wallet app with one code.


*Read also:*[QR Payments in Malaysia: A Complete Guide for Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-my/blog/qr-payments-in-malaysia-a-business-guide-to-accepting-duitnow/)


### **4. Credit and debit cards: essential for bigger tickets**


Cards still matter in Malaysia, particularly for travel, subscriptions, larger purchases, and international customers. Card use is growing, not shrinking: debit card transactions rose 20.5% in 2025 against 10.9% for credit cards, and contactless payments reached 2 billion transactions,


[according to BNM](https://www.malaymail.com/news/money/2026/03/31/contactless-and-duitnow-qr-transactions-rise-25pc-in-2025-malaysians-make-538-payments-each-on-average/214496) . Domestic debit cards run on MyDebit, PayNet's national debit scheme, alongside Visa and Mastercard.


Installments are a big part of the card story. Many Malaysian banks offer 0% installment plans that let cardholders spread a large purchase over months, which can lift conversion on electronics, furniture, and travel.


How it works:


the customer enters card details at checkout and usually completes a 3D Secure check with their bank. Cards can be saved for one-click and recurring billing, or converted into an installment plan at checkout.


When to offer it:


for SaaS and subscriptions, travel and hospitality, premium retail, and any business with foreign customers. With Xendit, you can accept


[Visa and Mastercard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards) , offer 0% installment plans from 11 banks over 6 to 60 months, and take Apple Pay on payment links.


*Read also:*[Card Payments in Malaysia: A Complete Guide for Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-my/blog/how-to-accept-credit-card-payments-in-malaysia-a-guide-for-businesses/)


### **5. Buy now, pay later (BNPL): small tickets, young shoppers**


BNPL has become a mainstream option for younger Malaysians. The Consumer Credit Oversight Board (CCOB) counted at least 6.5 million active BNPL accounts in the first half of 2025, with users aged 30 and below making around 40% of transactions. SPayLater held 56.5% of users, Atome 26.5%, and PayLater by Grab 8.3%, and the average BNPL transaction was below RM100, according to Fintech News Malaysia \[link needed\].


How it works:


the customer chooses a BNPL provider at checkout, is approved in seconds, and splits the payment into installments, often interest-free. The provider pays the merchant and carries the credit risk.


When to offer it:


for fashion, beauty, electronics, and lifestyle purchases aimed at Gen Z and millennial shoppers. Because the average ticket is small, BNPL in Malaysia works for everyday purchases, not only big-ticket items.


### **6. Bank transfer via virtual account: for large B2B payments**


For large payments, especially between businesses, a virtual account (VA) gives each customer or invoice its own account number. Every payment lands against that number, so it is matched to the right invoice automatically, with no proof-of-payment screenshots to chase.


How it works:


the customer receives a VA number and pays it by bank transfer from any bank. The payment is identified and confirmed automatically.


When to offer it:


for B2B invoicing, wholesale, property, and other high-value payments that exceed online banking limits. With Xendit, you can accept payments into an


[AmBank virtual account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/ambank-virtual-account) of up to RM10 million per transaction.


## **How to choose the right payment mix**


There is no single best method; the right mix depends on what you sell, your average order value, and whether customers pay once or repeatedly. As a baseline, FPX plus the major e-wallets covers most Malaysian online shoppers, and cards add the higher-value and international customers.

A few practical rules help whichever mix you choose. Show the most popular methods first on mobile. Offer both FPX and an e-wallet on every consumer checkout, since each covers shoppers the other misses. Track success and drop-off rates per method, then add or reorder options based on what your own customers use.

## **Frequently asked questions (FAQ)**


#### What is the most popular online payment method in Malaysia?


Online banking through FPX and DuitNow is the largest share of e-commerce value, at 44% in 2025, followed by e-wallets at 26%. Cards remain important for higher-value and international purchases.


#### What is the difference between FPX and DuitNow Pay?


Both let customers pay directly from their bank account and are run by PayNet. FPX is the long-established online banking gateway with separate retail and corporate channels. DuitNow Pay is the newer open-banking checkout that also covers digital banks.


#### Which e-wallets should I accept first?


Touch 'n Go eWallet, GrabPay, and ShopeePay cover most everyday Malaysian wallet users. Add WeChat Pay and Alipay if you serve tourists from China.


#### Is DuitNow QR only for physical stores?


No. It is most common in person, but customers can also scan a QR on a checkout page. It is linked with several countries, so tourists from Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, China, and Cambodia can pay with their home apps.


#### Which methods support recurring payments?


Cards and linked e-wallets (Touch 'n Go, GrabPay, and ShopeePay) can be charged again after the customer's first authorization, which makes them the best fit for subscriptions.
